prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

Genial poets, pink-faced earnest wits— you have given the world some choice morsels, gobbets of language presented as one presents T-bone steak and Cherries Jubilee. Goodbye, goodbye, I don’t care if I never taste your fine food again, neutral fellows, seers of every side. Tolerance, what crimes are committed in your name. And you, good women, bakers of nicest bread, blood donors. Your crumbs choke me, I would not want a drop of your blood in me, it is pumped by weak hearts, perfect pulses that never falter: irresponsive to nightmare reality. It is my brothers, my sisters, whose blood spurts out and stops forever because you choose to believe it is not your business. Goodbye, goodbye, your poems shut their little mouths, your loaves grow moldy, a gulf has split the ground between us, and you won’t wave, you’re looking another way. We shan’t meet again— unless you leap it, leaving behind you the cherished worms of your dispassion, your pallid ironies, your jovial, murderous, wry-humored balanced judgment, leap over, un- balanced? ... then how our fanatic tears would flow and mingle for joy ...

# A Farewell to Detached Perfection

Farewell, then, to the skilled poets and the practiced writers whose work I once may have admired. Your verses are polished to a flawless shine, your prose balanced with careful neutrality, but I bid you goodbye. What you offer now strikes me as nothing more than self-satisfied delicacies—refined confections that please the palate while nourishing nothing essential. I no longer value them, and I will no longer pretend that I do.

I have come to see your prized tolerance and your detached balance for what they truly are: a form of complicity. When you stand at a careful distance from suffering, weighing every side with equal calm, you are not being wise—you are being absent. Grave crimes are committed in the name of such supposed neutrality. The comfortable middle ground you occupy is not innocent; it is the very soil in which injustice takes root and flourishes unopposed.

So I reject the comfortable kindness of those who remain emotionally unresponsive to real suffering. You may extend to me your gentle words, your metaphorical bread and blood offered with a mild and untroubled hand—but I will not accept them. I cannot break bread with those whose hearts stay unmoved before the anguish of the living and the dying.

Understand this plainly: the deaths of my brothers and sisters are not accidents of fate. They are the direct result of bystanders who chose to believe that such tragedies were simply not their concern. Every averted gaze, every shrug of practiced indifference, becomes another blow struck against the vulnerable. Your silence is not empty—it has weight, and it has consequences.

And so I declare the divide between us, unbridgeable as it now stands. Between myself and the dispassionate there can be no easy peace. Yet I do not close the door entirely. Reconciliation remains possible—but only on one condition. Abandon your detached irony. Set down the cool remove that protects you from feeling. Commit yourself, passionately and without reservation, to my side. Do that, and we may yet stand together. Until then, I bid you farewell.

# On Complicity and the Failure of Neutrality

This poem mounts a fierce confrontation with two intertwined figures: the complacent poet who retreats into craft and detachment, and the comfortable citizen who hides behind the appealing virtues of neutrality, tolerance, and ironic distance. The speaker refuses to accept these postures as innocent. What presents itself as sophistication—the measured tone, the balanced view, the careful refusal to take sides—is unmasked as something far more troubling: a quiet participation in the very suffering it claims to observe from above.

To make this argument, the poem draws on a cluster of visceral metaphors. Food becomes an image of appetite and consumption, of those who feast while others starve, digesting the world's pain into comfortable nourishment. Blood insists on the physical reality of violence, the raw wound that irony cannot cauterize and that detachment only allows to flow unchecked. And through it all runs the image of a widening gulf—a chasm that grows between those who suffer and those who merely watch, between the engaged and the disengaged. This distance is not neutral ground; it is a moral abyss that the bystanders themselves deepen with every act of turning away.

The heart of the poem's indictment lies in its treatment of "balanced judgment." In ordinary discourse, we prize evenhandedness as a mark of wisdom and fairness. But the speaker exposes a darker truth: when confronted with genuine violence and injustice, the refusal to commit—the insistence on weighing all sides equally—is not impartiality but complicity. To stand back and pronounce careful, dispassionate verdicts while others bleed is to align oneself, however subtly, with the forces of harm. Passivity is not the absence of a choice; it is a choice, and a damning one.

Yet the poem does not close only in condemnation. Its fierceness carries within it the possibility of redemption. The speaker holds open a path to reconciliation—but only on a demanding condition. The comfortable poets and detached citizens must abandon their prized dispassion. They must climb down from the safe height of irony and neutrality and cross the widening gulf to stand alongside those who suffer. Only by committing themselves to a shared human struggle, by accepting the vulnerability and involvement they have so carefully avoided, can they be restored to genuine moral community. The offer is generous, but it demands nothing less than transformation: the end of watching and the beginning of belonging.

# A Genial Celebration: Cherries Jubilee

There's something truly special about desserts that bring warmth and joy to the table, and few do it quite as elegantly as Cherries Jubilee. This classic dish, with its rich history and dramatic presentation, has been delighting guests for generations.

## The Origins

Cherries Jubilee is believed to have been created by the legendary chef Auguste Escoffier, reportedly for one of Queen Victoria's Jubilee celebrations in the late 19th century. The dessert's name itself carries a sense of festivity and grandeur, making it perfect for marking special occasions.

## What Makes It Genial

The genius—or shall we say, the *genial* charm—of this dessert lies in its beautiful simplicity. At its heart, Cherries Jubilee combines just a few quality ingredients:

- **Fresh or preserved cherries**, plump and sweet
- **Sugar** to enhance their natural flavor
- **Brandy or kirsch** for that signature flambé
- **Vanilla ice cream** as the perfect cool companion

The result is a warm, luscious cherry sauce that pairs magnificently with creamy vanilla, creating a delightful contrast of temperatures and textures.

## The Showstopping Moment

What sets Cherries Jubilee apart is its theatrical flambé finale. When the warm cherries are doused with liquor and carefully ignited, blue flames dance across the pan, creating a spectacle that never fails to impress dinner guests. This genial display transforms a simple dessert into an unforgettable experience.

## A Timeless Treat

Whether you're hosting a dinner party or celebrating a milestone, Cherries Jubilee remains a wonderful choice. Its combination of elegant flavors, rich tradition, and genial spirit makes it a dessert worth revisiting—a true celebration on a plate that honors both its royal roots and the joy of good food shared with good company.

*So the next time you want to add a touch of jubilation to your table, consider this cheerful classic!*

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a poem in the voice of an angry political activist condemning moderate, "balanced" intellectuals and poets who stay neutral while people suffer and die.
counterfactuals.output:
**Neutral Ground**

You who weigh each word like a jeweler counts his gold,
who trim the candle of your rage to keep the room half-lit—
I have watched you fold your careful hands
and call it wisdom.

There is a body in the street.
You ask for context.
There is a mother screaming at the rubble.
You clear your throat and speak of *complexity,*
of how the truth lives somewhere in the middle,
as if the middle were a place
and not a locked door
you lean against
to keep the wind of it from touching you.

You call yourselves the reasonable ones,
the bridge, the balance, the both-sides scale—
but a scale needs a hand to hold it steady,
and yours has always tipped
toward whoever pours the wine.

Poet, where were your metaphors
when they came at dawn?
You who can find a hundred names for a sunset
had none for what was done in daylight.
You wrote of longing. You wrote of rain.
You wrote a thousand tender nothings
while the actual rain fell red
and someone's child learned the vocabulary of sirens.

Don't tell me art must float above the fray.
The fray is where the people are.
Your silence is not silence—
it is a vote,
a quiet ballot cast for the comfortable,
a signature scrawled across the warrant
in invisible, respectable ink.

I do not ask you to be simple.
I ask you to be *there.*
To let the injustice cost you something—
your dinner-party welcome,
your gentle reputation,
the smooth untroubled surface of your days.

There is no neutral ground.
There is only the ground
where the bodies fall,
and the balcony above it
where you stand,
admiring the arrangement of the light.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a free-verse poem addressed to comfortable, apolitical writers and "good" citizens, accusing them of complicity through their tolerance and detachment from real violence.
counterfactuals.output:
# The Comfortable

You who sleep well,
who write of gardens and the private ache
of love gone quiet in the evening—
I am speaking to you.

You who fold your hands
at the dinner table,
who pay your taxes clean and early,
who nod at the news and change the channel
when the bodies come—
I know your face.

It is a good face.
It is the face of someone
who has never had to run,
who mistakes silence for peace,
who mistakes distance for innocence.

You say: *I take no side.*
As if the fire asked your permission.
As if the man beneath the boot
could afford your neutral heart.
As if the space between action and inaction
were not itself a kind of hand
pressed gently on the drowning head.

You write your careful sentences,
each one a small locked room
with the curtains drawn against the street.
You call it craft.
You call it staying out of it.
I call it the long habit of looking away
until looking away becomes a spine,
a posture, a way of standing
so upright you cannot bend to see
what breaks below you.

Do not tell me you did not know.
The knowing was available.
It was printed, it was screaming,
it was carried on the wind
that also carried the scent of your good coffee.

You were not cruel.
That is the horror of it.
You were kind, and civil, and reasonable,
and the machine ran smoothly
on the oil of your reasonableness.

When they ask, later,
who let it happen—
and they will ask,
the children will ask
with their terrible clean eyes—
you will say *I only lived my life.*

And that
will be the truest, most damning thing
you ever wrote.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a poem in the style of Denise Levertov that attacks the tolerant, ironic, uncommitted literary establishment during a time of war and injustice.
counterfactuals.output:
**What Were We Made For**

Not the cool hands folded
over the well-set table,
not the raised eyebrow
that turns a scream
into a subject for discussion.

While the children are burning
you speak of ambiguity.
You have made a religion
of seeing every side,
until you cannot see
the one side bleeding
in the road.

I know your rooms—
the good wine, the good talk,
the poem that dares
nothing, risks nothing,
that folds its wings
and calls the folding *craft.*

You who are so amused,
so balanced on the fence
its wire cuts you clean
in two and you feel nothing—

there is a country
where the fence is barbed
and men die on it,
and no one there
admires your poise.

I want to break
the beautiful glass
of your detachment,
to make you stand
in the rubble
where irony is a luxury
the dead cannot afford.

Say it plainly:
*this is wrong.*
Say it without the shrug,
without the clever turn
that lets you off the hook
of being human.

The war goes on
because so many reasonable men
found reasons.
The injustice stands
because so many gentle voices
would not shout.

I am tired
of your tolerance
that tolerates
everything but conviction.

Choose. The hour
does not wait
for your considered response.
The house is burning
and you are annotating
the smoke.

---

*A note: I've written this as an original poem in Levertov's register—her use of direct address, her moral urgency during the Vietnam era, the short broken lines and the turn toward imperative. It's meant to echo the spirit of poems like "Life at War" rather than to reproduce any actual Levertov text.*
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a bitter farewell poem that uses food imagery—steak, cherries, bread, crumbs—to reject fellow poets and neutral people for their moral indifference.
counterfactuals.output:
**Farewell to the Comfortable**

I leave you to your steak, its blood gone cool,
you carvers of the quiet middle ground,
who dined while others starved outside the rule
and passed the salt without a single sound.

You plucked your cherries, spat the pits like verse,
made pretty rhymes of everything but this—
the burning street, the mother at the hearse—
and called your silence craft, and craft, and bliss.

You broke your bread with everyone the same:
the drowning and the drowner, side by side.
Neutrality, you wore it like a name,
a linen napkin folded over pride.

And you, my fellow poets, soft and fed,
who sharpened metaphors but not your spine—
you left the hungry ones your table's dread,
the crumbs of conscience swept beneath the wine.

I wanted more than aftertaste from you.
I wanted hands that shook, refused, or gave.
Instead you licked your plates and called it true,
and buried courage in a shallow grave.

So keep your cherries. Keep the marbled meat.
Keep every crumb you never thought to share.
I am done breaking bread across this seat—
I choose the ones who suffered, and who dared.

Goodbye. The feast was yours. The famine, ours.
May every full and easy mouth go dry.
I'll take the crust, the cold, the bitter hours,
before I'd toast your comfort. Here—goodbye.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Write an impassioned protest poem denouncing "balanced judgment" and detached irony, ending with a hopeful image of these neutral people finally leaping over to the side of committed action.
counterfactuals.output:
# The Fence-Sitters

You who weigh each atrocity
on scales of measured doubt,
who furrow brows at both the fire
and those who cry it out—

I am tired of your careful "yet,"
your reasonable "but,"
the way your open-minded stance
keeps every doorway shut.

You raise your ironic eyebrow high
at anyone who *feels*,
who dares to name a wound a wound,
who kneels where someone kneels.

You call it wisdom, this cool remove,
this permanent maybe—
while children learn what silence means
from your neutrality.

The tyrant loves your steady hand,
your "let us hear both sides,"
your dinner-party equanimity
where nothing quite decides.

For balance is a luxury
the drowning never own,
and irony's a comfort worn
by those who watch alone.

*Come down.* The air is thinner there
above the human fray.
Come down and get your fine coat torn
in the honest mud of day.

For there's a fence you've straddled long—
I've watched you perched and pale—
but look: the wind is changing now,
and even you can feel

the pull of some tremendous *yes*
too large to hold at bay—

*And there!* You're leaping! Both feet down
on the trembling, chosen ground—
you've landed loud among the ones
who love enough to *stay.*
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
